chapter: Growing up with jazz in Belfast
title: Ken Colyer and the Crane River Jazz Band
summary: He heard Colyer's band in London in 1949 and describes its Bunk-copying sound, instrumentation and records.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: He came in 53. Uh-huh. 53. Yeah. Uh, stayed for a few months, I think. But Collier, Collier's always, Collier got his hands on some American music records, when he was in the Merchant Navy in the war, and brought them home and they decided that this was the real jazz and he got this bunch of fellas together. He had another cornet playing with him, uh, Sonny Morris. And he got Monty Sunshine, who in those days played his kind of steel clarinet that he'd seen a photograph of George Lewis playing, you know. He played in a metal one?

And he played, tried to play, he used to play all, I remember I had an old record of Bunk playing Tishomingo blues on Brunswick and hear the Crane River band and they'd play every note identically, you know, an old clarinet phrase coming through. No drums, Collier was always very particular about drums, he said until he could find a drummer that was fit to play with a New Orleans band, he wasn't gonna have one. He just had a two string, three string bass, trombone, Julian Davis, he wore a fez, and Pat Hawes on the piano. They were very enthusiastic, they made a Hawes, H-A-W-E-S. Made a pretty sluggish sound, though, altogether. I got one of their records still, on a Delta label. Kentucky H-

and Moose March which is always copied straight from Russell's I think Russell's got one Moose March hasn't he or somebody's got one of punk he may have yeah I think so I think I've heard it somewhere I don't know whether it was Russell or one of those other early fellows that recorded down here and I heard them and I heard Littleton Littleton's band and that was much better to my mind it was much more lively much less much more imagination much looser they weren't in they weren't they didn't really worry if they deviated from the party line at all you know they are like them I don't think they've ever come up to what they were playing in those days they've changed a lot you see he's a man who believes in regrouping everything around he's trying to play mainstream now
